questions.stem_latex:
A teacher surveyed his class of 24 students about the subjects that they have chosen to study in the following year.

The results indicate that:

\begin{itemize}
\item 8 students chose to study neither Physics nor Chemistry
\item 8 students chose to study Chemistry
\item 12 students chose to study Physics.
\end{itemize}

parts.label: a
parts.latex: Draw a Venn diagram showing this information.

parts.label: b
parts.latex:
A student choosing to study Chemistry is event 1. A student choosing to study Physics is event 2.

If a student is chosen at random, determine whether these events are independent of each other.

parts.label: c
parts.latex:
The entire year group is given the same survey. The results indicate that:

\begin{itemize}
\item the probability that a student chose to study Chemistry is $\dfrac{1}{3}$
\item the probability that a student chose to study Physics is $\dfrac{2}{5}$
\item given that a student chose to study Chemistry, the probability that they chose to study Physics is $\dfrac{3}{7}$.
\end{itemize}

Calculate the probability that a student picked at random has chosen to study Chemistry or Physics.

B is correct. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is increasing on $(-\infty,0)$, decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, stationary at $x=0$, and $y\to 1$ as $x\to\pm\infty$. Hence $y=f'(x)$ must be above the $x$-axis on $(-\infty,0)$, below the $x$-axis on $(0,\infty)$, have an $x$-intercept at $x=0$, and $f'(x)\to 0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$.

A is incorrect because there is no $x$-intercept at $x=0$. C is incorrect because the graph is below the $x$-axis as $x\to-\infty$. D is incorrect because the graph does not approach the $x$-axis as $x\to\pm\infty$.

As $f(2x)$ is a horizontal dilation of $f(x)$ by a factor of $\dfrac12$, the area under the graph is halved:

$$\int_1^3 f(2x)\,dx = \dfrac12\int_2^6 f(x)\,dx = \dfrac32$$

Translating the graph three units to the right gives $\displaystyle\int_4^6 f(2(x-3))\,dx = \dfrac32$.

C is correct. Let $h(x) = f[g(x)]$. Then $h(-x) = f[g(-x)] = f[-g(x)] = f[g(x)]$ (since $g$ is odd, then $f$ is even), so $h(x)=h(-x)$ and $f[g(x)]$ is even.

A is incorrect: for $h(x)=f(x)\times g(x)$, $h(-x) = f(x)\times(-g(x)) = -h(x)$, so it is odd, not even.

B is incorrect: for $h(x)=f(x)+g(x)$, $h(-x) = f(x)-g(x)$, which is neither $h(x)$ nor $-h(x)$.

D is incorrect: for $h(x)=g[f(x)]$, $h(-x)=g[f(x)] = h(x)$, so it is even, not odd.

$$E(X) = \sum xp(x) = -\dfrac{1}{10}+b+5ab = -\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{11}{2}b-20b^2 \quad\text{for } 0\le b\le \dfrac{9}{40}$$

Smallest value: $b=0$ gives $E(X)=-\dfrac{1}{10}$. For the largest value, the vertex of the quadratic is at $b = \dfrac{11/2}{40} = \dfrac{11}{80}$, giving $E(X) = -\dfrac{1}{10}+\dfrac{11}{2}\left(\dfrac{11}{80}\right)-20\left(\dfrac{11}{80}\right)^2 = \dfrac{89}{320}$.

Therefore $-\dfrac{1}{10}\le E(X)\le\dfrac{89}{320}$.

$$100 = 200e^{-0.05t} \Rightarrow \dfrac12 = e^{-0.05t} \Rightarrow \ln\left(\dfrac12\right) = -0.05t \Rightarrow \ln2 = 0.05t \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{\ln2}{0.05} = 13.86\ldots\approx 14\text{ minutes}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: gives the correct solution; 1: correctly arrives at the expression $100=200e^{-0.05t}$ and attempts to solve for $t$

solutions.latex:
$\dfrac{dM_A}{dt} = -0.05\times200e^{-0.05t} = -10e^{-0.05t}$

$\dfrac{dM_B}{dt} = 400\times\ln3\times(-0.12)\times3^{-0.12t} = -48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$

Equate the two rates:

$$-10e^{-0.05t} = -48\ln3\times3^{-0.12t}$$
$$\dfrac{10}{48\ln3} = \dfrac{3^{-0.12t}}{e^{-0.05t}} = \dfrac{e^{(-0.12\ln3)t}}{e^{-0.05t}} = e^{(-0.12\ln3+0.05)t}$$
$$0.1895\ldots = e^{-0.0818\ldots t}$$
$$t = \dfrac{\ln0.1895\ldots}{-0.0818\ldots} = 20.317\ldots\text{ minutes}\approx 20\text{ minutes }19\text{ seconds}$$

Therefore, both substances decay at the same rate at 20 minutes and 19 seconds.

$$4\cos4x = \dfrac12\sin4x \Rightarrow 8\cos4x = \sin4x \Rightarrow 8 = \tan4x$$

$$\therefore \tan4x = 8$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: gives the correct solution

solutions.latex:
$\tan4x=8$ in $[0,4\pi]$: $4x = \tan^{-1}8,\ \left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right),\ \left(2\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$, so $x = \dfrac14\tan^{-1}8,\ \dfrac14\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right),\ \dfrac14\left(2\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$.

Therefore the solutions in the domain $[0,\pi]$ (first two) are $x_1 = \dfrac14\tan^{-1}8$ and $x_2 = \dfrac14\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: gives the correct solutions; 1: correctly shows ONE solution

solutions.latex:
$y = 10e^{-\frac12x}\sin4x$, so

$$y' = 10\left[\sin4x\times\left(-\dfrac12\right)e^{-\frac12x}+e^{-\frac12x}\times4\cos4x\right] = 10e^{-\frac12x}\left(-\dfrac12\sin4x+4\cos4x\right)$$

For stationary points $y'=0$: $e^{-\frac12x}=0$ (no real solutions as $e^{-\frac12x}>0$) or $-\dfrac12\sin4x+4\cos4x=0$. Therefore:

$$X_1 = \dfrac14\tan^{-1}8,\qquad X_2 = \dfrac14\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$$

Note: consequential on the answer to part (a)(ii).
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: gives the correct solution; 1: finds the derivative of $y$

solutions.latex:
When $X_1=\dfrac14\tan^{-1}8$: $Y_1 = 10e^{-\frac18\tan^{-1}8}\sin\left(\tan^{-1}8\right)$.

When $X_2=\dfrac14\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)$: $Y_2 = 10e^{-\frac18\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)}\sin\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right) = -10e^{-\frac18\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)}\sin\left(\tan^{-1}8\right)$.

Common ratio:

$$r = \dfrac{Y_2}{Y_1} = -e^{-\frac18\left(\pi+\tan^{-1}8\right)+\frac18\tan^{-1}8} = -e^{-\frac18\pi}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 3: gives the correct solution with $r=-e^{-\frac18\pi}$; 2: correctly finds an expression for $Y_1$ and $Y_2$; 1: correctly finds an expression for $Y_1$
